body:
Why girls' education was a social reform issue

In the 19th century, many girls had limited opportunities for formal education. Families sometimes feared that sending girls to school would conflict with domestic responsibilities or prevailing expectations about women's conduct.

Reformers argued that education would enable women to read, make informed decisions, support themselves and participate more fully in society.

Schools for girls developed in different regions, while some women learned at home or taught themselves. The growth of women's literacy helped create a new generation of women writers, teachers and social activists.

Important educational reformers

Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule

In Pune, Savitribai and Jyotirao Phule promoted education for girls and challenged the restrictions placed on marginalized communities. Their educational work was closely connected with the wider struggle against caste discrimination.

Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar

In Bengal, Vidyasagar supported the establishment of schools for girls. He combined efforts in women's education with his campaign for widow remarriage.

Mumtaz Ali and Muslim women's education

Mumtaz Ali argued in favour of women's education within Muslim society. He interpreted religious teaching to support women's opportunities to learn.

Education among Muslim women was not limited to one region or institution. The Begums of Bhopal also supported girls' education, including a primary school for girls at Aligarh.

Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain

Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain was a prominent advocate of Muslim women's education. She criticized ideas that treated women as intellectually inferior and established schools for girls.

Her Sakhawat Memorial Girls' School was established in Calcutta in 1911, following an earlier educational initiative at Bhagalpur.

Women began writing about their own lives

Education enabled women not only to receive knowledge but also to express independent opinions about inequality.

Tarabai Shinde and Stri Purush Tulana

Tarabai Shinde published Stri Purush Tulana, meaning A Comparison between Women and Men, in 1882.

She criticized the unequal standards applied to men and women. Her writing challenged the assumption that women alone should be blamed or punished for conduct tolerated among men.

Pandita Ramabai and widows' welfare

Pandita Ramabai was a Sanskrit scholar and social reformer who criticized restrictions on women, particularly the difficult conditions faced by many upper-caste Hindu widows.

She established institutions to educate and support women. Her Sharada Sadan, opened in 1889 in Bombay and subsequently associated with Pune, provided education and support to widows.

The purpose of such institutions extended beyond shelter. Education and training could help women acquire the skills needed for economic independence.

Three connected forms of change

Educational reform, women's writing and practical support institutions reinforced one another. Schools increased access to knowledge. Writing allowed women to criticize unequal customs publicly. Shelters and training institutions provided opportunities for women to act with greater independence.

Tarabai Shinde is associated with Stri Purush Tulana; Pandita Ramabai with the education and support of widows; Begum Rokeya with the advancement of Muslim girls' education.

Prelims focus

  • Savitribai Phule: Pioneering girls' education work in Pune.
  • Vidyasagar: Girls' education and widow remarriage in Bengal.
  • 1882: Tarabai Shinde published Stri Purush Tulana.
  • 1889: Pandita Ramabai established Sharada Sadan in Bombay.
  • 1911: Begum Rokeya's Sakhawat Memorial Girls' School in Calcutta.
  • Trap: Stri Purush Tulana and Sharada Sadan are associated with different reformers.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed pp. 98–99; Press Information Bureau, President of India's address to the 95th All India Marathi Literary Conference, 24 April 2022, paragraph identifying Tarabai Shinde's 1882 work, consulted 20 November 2026; Government of Maharashtra, historical material on Pandita Ramabai and Sharada Sadan, consulted 20 November 2026; Sakhawat Memorial Girls' School, institutional history, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Women discuss a manuscript while another prepares paper at a manual printing press in a modest late 19th-century Indian workspace.
pictures.caption: Women increasingly used writing and publication to challenge unequal social expectations.

pictures.alt: Girls' schooling, Tarabai Shinde's writing in 1882 and Pandita Ramabai's Sharada Sadan in 1889 contributed to greater opportunities for women's independence.
pictures.caption: Education, public expression and practical support worked together in women's reform.

title: Girls' Education, Women Reformers and the Growth of Women's Voices

body:
Two different legal questions

Campaigns against child marriage involved concern for girls' health, education and freedom from harmful social practices. Legal reform developed gradually, but different laws addressed different problems.

The age of consent concerned the minimum age relevant to criminal-law protection against sexual intercourse. The minimum age of marriage concerned the age at which a person could lawfully enter marriage under the applicable marriage-related law.

Because the two ideas are connected, their dates and age limits are often confused. They must nevertheless be studied separately.

Age of consent: An age threshold used in determining criminal liability for sexual intercourse under the law applicable at the time. Minimum marriage age: An age threshold used to regulate or prohibit marriage involving a person below the prescribed age.

Age of Consent Act, 1891

The Age of Consent Act, 1891 raised the relevant age of consent for girls under the Indian Penal Code from 10 to 12 years.

The reform concerned criminal-law protection, including in the context of child marriage. It did not establish a general minimum marriage age of 12 years or automatically invalidate every marriage involving a girl below that age.

This is the central distinction: a law could address sexual intercourse with a young girl without directly prohibiting the solemnization of her marriage.

Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929

The Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929 is commonly called the Sarda Act, after Harbilas Sarda, who was associated with the legislative initiative.

The Act received assent on 1 October 1929 and came into force on 1 April 1930.

In the original Act, a child was defined as:

  • A male below 18 years.
  • A female below 14 years.

The Act sought to restrain child marriages through penalties for specified persons involved in arranging or conducting such marriages. It was not simply another version of the Age of Consent Act.

Original 1929 Act: Below 18 years for males and below 14 years for females. These are the original statutory thresholds, not the ages introduced by later amendments.

Later changes to marriage-age limits

Marriage-age thresholds were increased through subsequent legislation. A major amendment in 1978 raised the prescribed ages under the child-marriage restraint law to 21 years for males and 18 years for females.

The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, which came into force in 2007, later replaced the earlier restraint legislation. At the content cutoff of 20 November 2026, the 2006 Act is the relevant central legislation and retains the male-below-21 and female-below-18 definition of a child. The historical 1929 age limits should not be mistaken for those of the later law.

Comparison of the key measures

Law or changeYearMain distinction
Age of Consent Act1891Raised relevant age of consent from 10 to 12
Child Marriage Restraint Act1929Originally below 18 for males and below 14 for females
Marriage-age amendment1978Raised thresholds to 21 for males and 18 for females
Prohibition of Child Marriage Act2006Replaced the earlier restraint framework; commenced in 2007

Prelims focus

  • 1891: Age of Consent Act; age raised from 10 to 12.
  • 1929: Child Marriage Restraint Act, commonly called the Sarda Act.
  • 1 April 1930: Commencement of the 1929 Act.
  • Original 1929 limits: Male below 18; female below 14.
  • 1978: Thresholds raised to 21 for males and 18 for females.
  • Trap: The Age of Consent Act regulated a different legal question from the Child Marriage Restraint Act.

[NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, Chapter 8, Women, Caste and Reform, printed p. 100, for the historical campaign against child marriage; historical account of the Age of Consent Act, 1891, in Age of Consent: Challenges and Contradictions of Sexual Violence Laws in India, section 2, consulted 20 November 2026; Child Marriage Restraint Act, Act XIX of 1929, original text, sections 1–2, India Code historical legislation, consulted 20 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, historical account of amendments to child-marriage legislation, consulted 20 November 2026; Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, sections 1–2, India Code, legislative status checked 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Consent age rose from 10 to 12 in 1891; marriage thresholds were male below 18 and female below 14 in 1929, then below 21 and 18 in 1978 and 2006.
pictures.caption: Consent-age reform and minimum-marriage-age reform followed different legal paths.

title: Age of Consent and Child Marriage: Distinguishing the Major Laws

body:
Why property rights mattered

Property rights influenced a woman's ability to support herself and make independent decisions. Without secure rights over land, housing or other resources, a widow or daughter could remain economically dependent on male relatives.

Reform of marriage customs did not automatically settle questions of inheritance. The legal history of widow remarriage and women's property rights therefore contains several separate stages.

The 1856 widow-remarriage law and property

The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856 permitted Hindu widow remarriage. However, its original section 2 provided that specified rights and interests held by a widow in her deceased husband's property would cease on her remarriage.

Other rights were protected subject to the Act's provisions; for example, a widow did not forfeit her own property merely because she remarried. The important point is that legal recognition of remarriage did not create unrestricted inheritance rights.

Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937

The Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 improved the position of certain Hindu widows in inheritance.

In circumstances covered by the Act, a widow could receive a share or interest in property connected with her deceased husband. However, the right given under section 3 was generally a limited interest, traditionally described as a Hindu woman's estate.

A limited interest was not the same as full, unrestricted ownership. The widow's ability to deal with the property remained subject to legal limitations.

Hindu Succession Act, 1956

The Hindu Succession Act, 1956 introduced a major change in Hindu inheritance law.

Its section 14 established the general rule that property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the Act, would be held by her as a full owner rather than a limited owner, subject to section 14(2), which preserves a restricted estate where a gift, will, other instrument, civil-court decree or order, or award creates a new property right with that restriction rather than recognizing a pre-existing right.

This was a significant development because it moved away from the earlier framework of the limited Hindu woman's estate.

Hindu Succession Amendment, 2005

The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005 strengthened daughters' rights in joint family property governed by the Mitakshara system.

Under the amended section 6, a daughter of a coparcener becomes a coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son, with the same rights and liabilities in coparcenary property as a son, including the right to demand partition.

A coparcener is a member of a Hindu joint family who has an interest in coparcenary property under the applicable law. The 2005 amendment is especially important because it addressed daughters' rights in that form of joint family property.

The change should not be confused with the 1956 rule concerning a woman's ownership of property already possessed by her. The two reforms dealt with different legal questions.

Property-rights chronology

YearLegal developmentCentral point
1856Hindu Widows' Remarriage ActRemarriage permitted, with specified property consequences
1937Hindu Women's Rights to Property ActImproved certain widows' inheritance interests, generally as limited estates
1956Hindu Succession ActSection 14: general rule of full ownership for property possessed by a female Hindu
2005Hindu Succession AmendmentSection 6: daughters become coparceners by birth under Mitakshara law

These provisions concern the legal framework of Hindu inheritance and its specified applications. They should not be presented as a single inheritance rule that applies identically to every religious community in India.

Prelims focus

  • 1856: Widow remarriage legalized, but specified property rights could cease on remarriage.
  • 1937: Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act; generally limited interests for certain widows.
  • 1956, section 14: General rule of full ownership of property possessed by a female Hindu.
  • 2005, amended section 6: Daughter becomes a Mitakshara coparcener by birth in the same manner as a son.
  • Trap: The 1956 ownership provision and the 2005 coparcenary amendment are not the same legal reform.

[Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act, 1856, sections 1–2 and 5, historical statutory text, consulted 20 November 2026; Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, section 3, India Code historical legislation, consulted 20 November 2026; Hindu Succession Act, 1956, section 14, India Code, consulted 20 November 2026; Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, amended section 6, official statutory text; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Law and Justice release dated 9 September 2005, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline distinguishes remarriage in 1856, limited widow inheritance in 1937, full ownership in 1956 and daughters’ coparcenary rights in 2005.
pictures.caption: Widows' inheritance interests, women's ownership and daughters' coparcenary rights developed in separate stages.

title: Women's Property Rights: From Restricted Inheritance to Stronger Legal Ownership
